title: Vietnamese-Style Shrimp Bánh Xèo with Bean Sprouts & Herbs
dek: Lacy, turmeric-gold rice crêpes turn audibly crisp around juicy shrimp and bean sprouts, then tuck into herbs and rice paper with a bright chile-lime dipping sauce.
image_alt: Turmeric-yellow Vietnamese bánh xèo filled with shrimp and bean sprouts beside herbs, cucumber, rice paper and red chile dipping sauce
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups (240 g) white rice flour, not glutinous rice flour
2 tbsp cornstarch
1 tsp ground turmeric
3/4 tsp fine sea salt, divided
3/4 cup full-fat canned coconut milk, stirred
1 3/4 cups ice-cold water, plus 1 to 2 tbsp if needed
4 scallions, thinly sliced, white and green parts separated
12 oz medium raw shrimp, peeled, deveined and tails removed
1/4 tsp ground black pepper
1 small yellow onion, halved and very thinly sliced
4 cups mung bean sprouts, rinsed and dried well
6 tbsp neutral high-heat oil, such as avocado or rice bran oil, divided
1/4 cup warm water, for the dipping sauce
3 tbsp granulated sugar
1/4 cup fish sauce
1/4 cup fresh lime juice
1 garlic clove, finely grated
1 small red Thai chile, thinly sliced, seeded for less heat
1/4 cup finely shredded carrot
16 small round rice-paper wrappers (about 6 inches), for serving
1 small head butter lettuce, leaves separated, washed and dried
1 cup packed mixed mint and cilantro leaves
1 English cucumber, cut into thin matchsticks

instructions.name: Whisk and rest the rice batter
instructions.text: Whisk the rice flour, cornstarch, turmeric and 1/2 teaspoon salt in a large bowl. Add the coconut milk and ice-cold water gradually, whisking until no dry pockets remain. Stir in the scallion greens. Rest the thin batter for 30 minutes at room temperature so the flour hydrates; whisk again before every crêpe because rice flour settles quickly. It should run from the whisk like light cream, so add 1 to 2 tablespoons water if it has thickened.

instructions.name: Mix the chile-lime dipping sauce
instructions.text: While the batter rests, stir the warm water and sugar in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves. Stir in the fish sauce, lime juice, garlic, chile and shredded carrot. The sauce should taste bright, salty-sweet and pourable; set it aside so the garlic and chile can infuse while the crêpes cook.

instructions.name: Season and organize the filling
instructions.text: Pat the shrimp very dry, then toss with the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt, black pepper and scallion whites. Divide the shrimp, sliced onion and bean sprouts mentally into eight portions and arrange them beside the stove. Keep the lettuce, herbs, cucumber and dry rice paper away from the raw-shrimp work area, then wash the board, knife, bowl and your hands with hot soapy water.

instructions.name: Cook the shrimp in two batches
instructions.text: Heat a 10-inch nonstick or well-seasoned carbon-steel skillet over medium-high for 2 minutes. Add 1 teaspoon oil and half the shrimp, spreading them in one layer. Cook 60 to 90 seconds per side, until the thickest shrimp reaches 145°F and the flesh is firm, pearly and opaque. Transfer to a clean plate and repeat with another teaspoon oil and the remaining shrimp. Do not return cooked shrimp to the raw-shrimp bowl.

instructions.name: Sizzle the first thin crêpe
instructions.text: Wipe out loose scallion bits, return the skillet to medium-high and add 2 teaspoons oil. Scatter one-eighth of the onion across the pan. Whisk the batter, measure a scant 1/3 cup and pour it at the skillet's upper edge while immediately tilting and rotating the pan to coat the bottom in the thinnest possible layer. The batter should sizzle on contact and may leave a few lacy gaps; do not patch them with more batter.

instructions.name: Steam the sprouts, then crisp uncovered
instructions.text: Arrange one-eighth of the cooked shrimp and 1/2 cup bean sprouts over one half of the crêpe. Cover, lower the heat to medium and cook for 2 minutes so the sprouts soften but stay crisp. Uncover and cook for 3 to 4 minutes more, rotating the skillet once, until the rim curls away from the pan and the underside is deep golden and rigid enough to lift in one piece. Drizzle 1/2 teaspoon oil around a pale edge if it needs help crisping.

instructions.name: Fold and repeat without stacking
instructions.text: Slip a thin spatula under the empty half and fold it over the filling. Slide the bánh xèo onto a wire rack set over a sheet pan; do not stack or cover it, which traps steam. Repeat with the remaining batter, onion, shrimp and sprouts, whisking the batter before each scant 1/3-cup measure and adding 2 teaspoons oil per crêpe. Hold finished crêpes on the rack in a 225°F oven for no longer than 20 minutes while you finish the batch.

instructions.name: Wrap with herbs and serve immediately
instructions.text: Set out the hot bánh xèo with the dipping sauce, rice paper, lettuce, herbs and cucumber. Dip one rice-paper wrapper briefly in room-temperature water, wait about 30 seconds for it to become flexible, then layer on lettuce, herbs, cucumber and a torn strip of crisp crêpe. Roll snugly and dip into the chile-lime sauce. Alternatively, skip the rice paper and wrap pieces directly in lettuce.

why_it_works: Rice flour supplies a brittle, shattering shell without gluten, while a small amount of cornstarch reduces toughness and helps the thin edge turn lacy.
Cold liquid and a 30-minute rest fully hydrate the flour without warming it; whisking before each pour keeps settled starch from making the last crêpes dense.
A thoroughly preheated, lightly oiled pan creates the characteristic sizzle, and one quick tilt spreads a scant measure before the batter sets.
Covering briefly cooks the bean sprouts with trapped steam, then uncovering drives that moisture away so the base can become crisp instead of leathery.
Cooking the shrimp first gives a reliable 145°F safety check and prevents the crêpe from burning while thick raw shrimp struggle to cook through.
swaps: For a pork-and-shrimp version, replace 4 ounces of shrimp with 4 ounces very thinly sliced pork shoulder. Cook the pork to at least 145°F with a 3-minute rest before assembling the crêpes.

For a vegetarian version, replace the shrimp and fish sauce with 12 ounces pressed firm tofu and vegan fish sauce or light soy sauce. Brown the tofu before making the crêpes and season the sauce to taste because soy sauce is saltier by volume.
Perilla, Thai basil or mustard greens can join or replace part of the mint and cilantro; keep at least one sturdy leaf for wrapping and one aromatic herb for contrast.

Use eight large lettuce leaves instead of rice paper for a lighter, fully gluten-free wrap. If gluten matters, verify the fish sauce, cornstarch and rice-paper labels because cross-contact varies by brand.
A well-seasoned 10-inch carbon-steel skillet can replace nonstick. Preheat it fully and use the listed oil; stainless steel is much less forgiving with this low-fat rice batter.
storage: Bánh xèo are crispest straight from the skillet. Refrigerate leftover crêpes in a single layer between parchment in an airtight container at 40°F or below for up to 2 days; refrigerate the dipping sauce separately for up to 4 days and the washed herbs and lettuce for up to 2 days. Reheat crêpes uncovered on a wire rack in a 400°F oven for 7 to 9 minutes, or in a lightly oiled skillet over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes per side, until the shrimp filling reaches 165°F. Do not microwave them unless a soft texture is acceptable. Do not freeze assembled crêpes because the sprouts release water and the shell cracks.
notes: Vietnam Tourism's official home-recipe booklet pairs a coconut-and-turmeric batter with shrimp, bean sprouts, onion, greens, cucumber, rice paper and dipping sauce. This independently developed version specifies a measured rice-flour batter, separate shrimp safety check and repeatable 10-inch-skillet technique.

The word xèo evokes the audible sizzle as batter hits a hot pan. If the first pour is quiet, let the empty pan heat another 30 to 60 seconds before continuing; if the batter smokes or blackens, reduce the heat slightly.
The FDA advises cooking most seafood to 145°F; properly cooked shrimp also becomes firm, pearly and opaque. A thin probe inserted sideways into the thickest shrimp gives the most useful reading.
Do not soak the rice paper until limp. A quick dip followed by a short wait lets it finish softening on the plate without becoming sticky or tearing around the crisp crêpe.

Calories and cost estimate two bánh xèo, four rice-paper wrappers, vegetables, herbs and one quarter of the dipping sauce per serving. Exact values vary with oil absorption, shrimp size and local herb prices.

faqs.q: Why is my bánh xèo soft instead of crisp?
faqs.a: The skillet may be too cool, the batter may be too thick or the covered stage may have run too long. Preheat until a drop of batter sizzles immediately, use only a scant 1/3 cup in a 10-inch pan, tilt once and uncover after 2 minutes. Keep finished crêpes unstacked on a rack so their steam can escape.

faqs.q: Can I prepare the batter or fillings ahead?
faqs.a: Yes. Refrigerate the batter in a covered container for up to 24 hours and whisk it thoroughly before cooking, adding a spoonful of cold water if it has thickened. The sauce can be made 4 days ahead. Cook and chill the shrimp no more than 1 day ahead, but rinse and dry the sprouts and herbs the day you serve them for the best texture.

faqs.q: Do I need a special bánh xèo pan?
faqs.a: No. A 10-inch nonstick skillet gives the most repeatable home result because its sloped sides help the thin crêpe release and fold. A seasoned carbon-steel pan also works. Use the same pan for every crêpe, keep the batter measure consistent and adjust the burner only if the edges darken before the center sets.
